Subject: Private VPC: erase / residency questions

Hi Rachel,

Thanks for the demo last week — the team at AcmeCorp is most interested in the Private VPC option but we need to finalize our data handling commitments before we can sign. A few short questions from our security team: 

- Can Redwood guarantee that customer-managed storage (S3) in our VPC is the only copy of tenant customer data? Are there any caches, backups, or logs that live outside our VPC under normal operation?
- What is the standard retention window for request/response logs? Can we shorten that for our tenancy?
- If AcmeCorp requests a full tenant wipe, what is the step-by-step timeline and what evidence / attestation do you provide?
- Do you support on-demand cryptographic key rotation and the ability for us to revoke keys (KMS) to make old data unreadable?

We also need a short procedural playbook (one-page) and an example attestation statement to include in procurement. Can you pull that together or point me to where it already exists?

Appreciate it — Lisa

Hi Lisa — thanks for the clear list. I'm looping in Marissa (Product) and Vivek (Infra) to ensure we give operational details and the runbook. High-level answers below and we'll follow up with the playbook and an attestation draft attached.

Summary answers:
- Customer-managed storage: For Private VPC deployments the canonical store for tenant objects and logs is the S3 bucket that you control in your VPC. Redwood's control plane (when used) retains metadata pointers only; we do not mirror customer data outside the VPC by default.
- Caches / backups: We use ephemeral in-memory KV caches on the serving fleet for inference. Those caches are process-local and never persist to external storage. Standard backups (point-in-time) are disabled for customer buckets unless mutual agreement is reached; we can enable short retention object locking only if you request it.
- Retention window: Default operational request/response logs are 30 days for diagnostic purposes. We can reduce this to 0/7/14/30 per tenancy; we also support a configurable policy that enforces minimum retention to meet audit needs.
- Tenant wipe: We provide an on-demand tenant-erase API that deletes objects from the customer bucket and triggers a coordinated purge of indexing and metadata. Typical end-to-end completes in 48–72 hours for medium-size tenants (under 5TB) and we provide an attestation PDF + deletion audit log (timestamps + object counts). For larger datasets we provide a phased plan and SLA in the SOW.
- KMS: We integrate with customer-managed KMS (AWS KMS) keys. You can rotate/revoke keys; revocation will render prior-encrypted objects unreadable. We recommend a combined approach: revoke + run physical object-delete for full cryptographic assurance.

Attached: erase_playbook_v1.3.docx (playbook draft), acmecorp_sow_vpc.pdf (SOW excerpt with retention options).

Would you like a short call to walk the security team through the playbook? We can also provide an example attestation statement for procurement.

Thanks,

Thanks Rachel — a few clarifications from our audit checklist (excerpted):

1) We need explicit confirmation that there are no cold backups or snapshot copies of tenant objects retained by Redwood in any external account after provisioning.
2) For ephemeral caches: can you confirm the absence of persisting to EBS / networked storage in edge cases (e.g., OOM or crash dump behavior)?
3) For the attestation, we will need a signed statement on Redwood letterhead that includes: scope (tenant id), timestamp of wipe, list of deleted buckets/prefixes, and the name/email of the person who ran the wipe.

Finally — what are the controls around retention policy rollback? If Acme sets retention = 7 days and later asks to extend to 30 days, is that reversible? We prefer change control that prevents silent escalation of retention.

Tom/Lisa — thanks for the checklist. Below are technical specifics that should address the audit items, and I'll flag the portions you asked to include in the attestation template.

1) Backups & snapshots: Redwood does not take external backups of tenant object storage for Private VPC deployments by default. Any snapshot/backups are explicitly part of a managed-disaster-recovery addendum and must be opt-in. We never copy objects into Redwood-managed S3 buckets without customer authorization. (Attestation: "Redwood confirms no external backups exist for tenant <tenant-id> as of strike date, unless specified in the SOW.")

2) Ephemeral caches: Serving nodes use process-local RAM and in-memory KV structures. In the event of OOM/crash, core dumps are disabled for serving processes and we have a policy to scrub any temporary files on restart. Edge-case persistence to local disks is prohibited in our private deployment packaging; Vivek can confirm the packaging details below.

3) Erase flow (high-level):
- Customer initiates tenant erase via API or support ticket; authenticated operator + 2FA required.
- System flags tenant state -> QUIESCENT and rejects new writes.
- Asynchronous job enumerates objects/prefixes in your bucket(s) and issues delete operations.
- Metadata indexes in Redwood control plane (if used) are swept and tombstoned.
- Final verification job retries deletes and confirms zero object counts.
- Attestation generated: includes tenant id, deleted prefixes, counts, job run ids, timestamp, operator.

Expected timelines: 0–48 hours for tenants < 5TB; up to 7 days for large archival sets. All deletes are logged. (Attestation excerpt attached.)

4) Retention policy rollback: Retention changes are auditable and require an entitlements change. By default retention can be decreased (shorter window) immediately. Increasing retention (longer window) for already-deleted objects is not possible; extending retention only affects new objects. We can also lock a retention floor via policy so only approved admins can extend.

I've attached a draft attestation paragraph we usually include in procurement. If you confirm the wording we'll produce a signed PDF on letterhead.

—Marissa
Product Lead, Redwood Inference

Tom/Lisa — Vivek from infra here with runbook-level details and a note on edge cases. Attaching the operational playbook (erase_playbook_v1.3.docx). Key points: 

- Storage model: Customer S3 buckets in your AWS account are the authoritative copy. We mount/operate connectors (IAM role) but never copy data into Redwood-managed EBS/S3.
- Delete implementation: We use multipart-aware delete to ensure large objects are removed; we also scrub multipart upload remnants.
- Crash safety: serving containers run read-only rootfs; temp directories are union-mounted onto ephemeral instance store; no write-through to EBS. In any crash scenario there are no persistent cores or dumps containing PII.
- KMS behavior: We honor customer KMS keys; when you rotate or revoke a key, older ciphertext becomes unreadable. We additionally recommend running the object-delete job after key revocation for full assurance.
- Audit evidence: After a wipe we produce: deletion job ids, per-prefix object counts before/after, S3 API delete event receipts, and a signer identity (Redwood operator). We sign the attestation (PDF) with our corporate key and include the audit JSON.

Operational playbook (high level):
1) Customer opens support ticket or calls API -> ticket created in Redwood CS queue (owner + SLA).
2) Infra schedules a dedicated deletion job; operator initiates after 2FA confirmation.
3) Automated enumerator + parallel delete tasks run; retries are logged.
4) Post-delete verification and attestation generation.
5) Deliver attestation and audit bundle via secure Drive link or encrypted email.

Edge case: If clients had opted into cross-account snapshotting (again, opt-in only) we would enumerate and delete snapshots per SOW.

If you want, we can perform a dry-run on a small prefix to show the artifact bundle. Reach out with a date/time and we'll schedule.

—Vivek
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference
